title: Ladybugs Among the Leaves
description: Look closely at a ladybug through its beetle body, spotted wing covers, and tiny prey.
cardDescription: Look closely at a ladybug through its beetle body, spotted wing covers, and tiny prey.
focus: Ladybugs are beetles, and their hard forewings cover a separate flying pair. The clues distinguish the adult body from younger stages and from the insects it may eat.
solvingTip: Use the number or position of a body part. A covering, a feeler, and a food animal have different names.
words: American name for a small rounded beetle often marked with spots
One hardened beetle forewing covering the folded flying wings
Small plant-feeding insect eaten by many ladybugs
Immature feeding stage before a ladybug becomes a pupa
One paired feeler on a ladybug's head
Insect group characterized by hardened forewing covers
Small contrasting mark on many ladybug wing covers
Thin flight surface folded beneath a beetle's hard cover
Plant surface on which a ladybug may search for prey
One of an insect's six walking limbs
Body region carrying a ladybug's eyes and feelers
Early ladybug life stage often laid near a food supply
Stage between larva and adult in a ladybug's life cycle

answerNotes.LADYBUG: Ladybugs are beetles; not every species has the familiar red background with black spots.
answerNotes.ELYTRON: Elytron is singular, while elytra is plural; these hard covers are modified forewings.
answerNotes.APHID: Many ladybugs prey on aphids, though not every species has the same diet.
answerNotes.LARVA: A ladybug larva looks different from the rounded adult beetle.
answerNotes.ANTENNA: Antennae are sensory structures, separate from the six walking legs.

title: An Ant Colony Under the Path
description: Explore an ant colony through its members, underground chambers, and food-gathering activity.
cardDescription: Explore an ant colony through its members, underground chambers, and food-gathering activity.
subtheme: An Ant Colony Under the Path
focus: Ant colonies organize work among different individuals. The clues identify roles and structures without treating a colony’s queen as a human-style commander.
solvingTip: Separate the animal’s role from the space it occupies and the route it follows.
words: Social insect commonly living in an organized colony
Reproductive female in an ant colony
Usually nonreproductive female performing an ant colony's daily tasks
Community of ants living and functioning together
Passage connecting spaces in an underground ant nest
Enlarged roomlike space within an ant nest
Route followed by a line of food-gathering ants
Home structure occupied by an ant colony
Ground material excavated by many nesting ants
Legless young stage cared for by adult ants
Developing stage before an ant emerges as an adult
Material gathered to nourish the colony
Mouthpart used by an ant for gripping or carrying
Chemical signal helping many ants follow a route

answerNotes.ANT: Ants are insects with six legs; their colonies vary greatly in size and behavior.
answerNotes.QUEEN: A queen's primary role is reproduction, not issuing commands like a human monarch.
answerNotes.WORKER: Worker ants perform jobs such as foraging and brood care; the exact division varies among species.
answerNotes.COLONY: Colony names the social group rather than just its underground nest structure.
answerNotes.TUNNEL: A tunnel is a connecting route; a chamber is an enlarged space reached along it.

title: An Earthworm in the Garden Soil
description: Study an earthworm through its ringed body, movement, and the soil structures it leaves behind.
cardDescription: Study an earthworm through its ringed body, movement, and the soil structures it leaves behind.
subtheme: An Earthworm in the Garden Soil
focus: Earthworms move using muscles and small bristles. Their body segments and reproductive band have particular names, while the burrow and cast are effects of their activity.
solvingTip: Distinguish a body feature from a tunnel or a deposit left in the ground.
words: Segmented animal commonly burrowing through garden soil
Thickened band on a mature earthworm associated with reproduction
One repeated division of an earthworm's body
One small bristle helping an earthworm grip its surroundings
Soil-rich material deposited after passing through an earthworm
Passage made by an earthworm through the ground
Earthy material through which a garden worm moves
Body tissue that contracts to move the worm
Circular outline suggested by a worm's repeated divisions
Slightly wet condition associated with active earthworms
Fallen plant material consumed by some earthworms
Small protective case containing developing earthworm eggs
Informal name for the rear end of the worm
Narrow passage through a garden bed's ground

answerNotes.EARTHWORM: Earthworms are annelids rather than insects; their body organization differs from an insect's six-legged form.
answerNotes.CLITELLUM: The clitellum helps form a cocoon for eggs; it is a body region rather than a separate ring-shaped animal.
answerNotes.SEGMENT: Segments make the body appear ringed; the entire worm is one animal.
answerNotes.SETA: Seta is singular and setae is plural; these bristles assist movement without being jointed legs.
answerNotes.CAST: A cast is a deposit, whereas a burrow is the passage in which a worm moves.

title: A Spider at Its Web
description: Explore a web-building spider through its silk, body parts, and the insects caught nearby.
cardDescription: Explore a web-building spider through its silk, body parts, and the insects caught nearby.
focus: Spiders are arachnids, not insects. The clues identify their silk-making structures and web features while recognizing that different spiders use different hunting methods.
solvingTip: Check whether the clue names the animal, a body part, or a silk structure.
words: Eight-legged arachnid that may catch prey in a web
Silk-spinning structure on a spider's abdomen
Animal group containing spiders and scorpions
Fiber produced by a spider for webs and other uses
Circular web form with spokes and a spiral
Silken structure spun by a web-building spider
One of a spider's eight walking limbs
Animal caught and eaten by a hunting spider
Single fine strand in a spider's web
Silken case surrounding a spider's eggs
Pointed mouthpart through which a spider can deliver venom
Small winged insect that may be caught in a web
Light-detecting body part on a spider's head region
Winding line crossing the spokes of an orb web

answerNotes.SPIDER: Not every spider builds a prey-catching web; web-building is one hunting strategy within the group.
answerNotes.SPINNERET: Spinnerets release silk from silk-producing glands; they are distinct from legs or mouthparts.
answerNotes.ARACHNID: Arachnids are separate from insects; adult spiders have eight legs rather than six.
answerNotes.SILK: Spider silk serves several purposes, including egg sacs and safety lines as well as prey capture.
answerNotes.ORB: Orb describes one web design; other spiders make sheets, tangles, or no capture web.

title: A Snail on a Garden Wall
description: Look at a land snail through its shell, muscular foot, and slow movement across a damp surface.
cardDescription: Look at a land snail through its shell, muscular foot, and slow movement across a damp surface.
subtheme: A Snail on a Garden Wall
focus: A snail’s shell grows with the animal. The clues separate the shell’s opening and tip from the soft body parts used for movement and sensing.
solvingTip: Use where the part is located: at the shell opening, at its pointed end, or beneath the animal.
words: Slow-moving mollusk carrying a coiled shell
One complete turn in a snail shell's coil
Opening through which a snail extends its soft body
Soft feeler extending from a snail's head
Pointed earliest-formed tip of a coiled snail shell
Hard outer structure carried by a snail
Muscular lower body surface used for crawling
Everyday name for the mucus left along a snail's route
Curving shape winding around the shell's center
Front body region bearing a snail's feelers
Moist surface condition on a shaded garden wall
Plant part grazed by some garden snails
Line of mucus left behind a moving snail
Vertical garden surface on which a snail may crawl

answerNotes.SNAIL: A snail is a mollusk rather than an insect; its broad muscular foot helps it move.
answerNotes.WHORL: A whorl is one turn of the growing shell, not the whole spiral structure.
answerNotes.APERTURE: Aperture means opening here; the same word appears in optical instruments with another context.
answerNotes.TENTACLE: Tentacles serve sensory roles; they are not jointed insect antennae.
answerNotes.APEX: The apex is at the shell's tip, while the aperture is its larger body opening.
